title: Feedback That Changes What Happens Next

audience.who: Corporate employees who give feedback to peers, reports or managers
audience.knows: How it feels to give and receive feedback; has softened or blurred a message to keep the peace
audience.cares_about: Saying the hard thing once, keeping the relationship, and actually seeing the behaviour change

outcome: Before a feedback conversation, the viewer can rewrite a vague or feelings-only comment into one that names a specific observed behaviour, its impact, and a concrete next step the other person can act on this week.
through_line: Feedback changes behaviour only when the other person leaves knowing exactly what to do differently; kindness or bluntness in delivery matters far less than whether the next action is clear.

arc_plan.what: Open on one running scene: a colleague gives a teammate well-meant feedback about their project updates, the teammate feels fine, and the next update is just as unclear. The viewer recognises the gap between a good conversation and no change.
Promise one rewrite move the viewer can apply to that same comment so the teammate's next update is different, framed as what they will be able to do, not an agenda.
Section one: replay the original comment and show why it fails, it judges the person or describes a feeling but names no observable behaviour, so the teammate cannot tell what to repeat or stop.

Section two: rebuild the same comment step by step on screen, adding the specific behaviour seen, its effect on the work or team, and one concrete next step agreed together, so the idea is named only after it is seen.
Show a new short vague comment from a different workplace moment and ask the viewer to spot which part is missing before revealing a rewritten version, a check they can genuinely pass or fail.
Prompt the viewer to pick one piece of feedback they owe someone this week and draft the next-step sentence before the conversation.
Return to the opening scene: the rewritten feedback is given, and the teammate's next update visibly changes, closing the loop between conversation and behaviour.

must_cover.what: Feedback aimed at feelings or character rather than observable behaviour rarely changes what the person does next
Name a specific behaviour that was actually observed, not a judgement or label
Connect the behaviour to its concrete impact on the work, team or outcome
End with a clear, agreed next action the person can take, not just an opinion
Inviting the other person's view as part of agreeing the next step

must_avoid: Statistics or research claims without a source on the knowledge sheet
Invented remarks attributed to real experts or companies
Opening by explaining what the word feedback means, or with an agenda slide
Presenting a named feedback model as established fact unless the knowledge sheet supports it
A tour of several unrelated examples that each appear once
Lecturing or scolding tone toward the viewer
Framing feedback as only for managers giving it downward
example_posture: One fictional running example carries the whole lesson: a teammate whose project updates are unclear and the colleague who gives them feedback. Keep it ordinary, believable and neutral in gender and role seniority. The check uses one second, brief workplace moment. Invented characters and lines are clearly illustrative, never presented as real people or real statements.
visual_direction: A person in a recognisable office situation that returns at the start and end; a before and after of the same feedback sentence, rebuilt piece by piece on one board; a small visible signal of change, such as the next update arriving clearer. One loud thing on screen at a time, light and warm rather than comic.
voice_note: The mentor speaks as an experienced colleague who has given clumsy feedback too, candid and practical, never preachy. Short sentences, one idea per line, warmth without softening the point.
open_questions: The look question was not answered; the request names a cartoon story style, so the classic treatment of that style is assumed, with a newer treatment offered later
Should the running example show feedback given upward or between peers, rather than manager to report?
Is there a house feedback framework or company language the video should align with?
